K.Natarajan vs S.Sudarsanan on 7 January, 2016

Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/6412785/
1
O R D E R

The second accused in C.C. No.8 of 1993 on the files of the Court of the Additional Chief Judicial Magistrate, Thiruvananthapuram filed this Revision Petition challenging the concurrent finding of conviction and sentence passed by the courts below under Sections 2(ia)
(a)(f), 7(i) and 16(1)(a)(i) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954 (for short 'the PFAAct').
2. Heard.
3.

The prosecution allegation can be briefly stated thus:-
On 7.11.1992 at about 11.30 a.m., PW1, the Food Inspector purchased 750 grams of dhall channa from the shop of the revision petitioner.
First accused was the salesman of the said shop.
Third accused supplied the item to the second accused.
Samples were taken in accordance with law and thereafter, one of the samples was sent for analysis to the Public Analyst.
The Public Analyst filed Ext. P13 report stating that the food item was adulterated.
4. Before the trial Court, PW1 to PW5 were examined and Exts.
P1 to P29 were marked for the prosecution.
DW1 to DW3 were examined and Exts.D1 to D8(a) were marked for the revision petitioner.

5. The learned counsel for the revision petitioner has submitted that since no laboratory was defined and no validated method of analysis was prescribed as provided under Section 23 (1-A)(ee) and (hh)
of the PFAAct, Ext. P13 cannot be acted upon to hold that the food item purchased by the Food Inspector was adulterated.
The learned counsel for the revision petitioner relied on the decision of the Apex Court in Pepsico India Holdings (P) Ltd. v. Food Inspector [(2011) 1 SCC 176] to buttress his argument.

entities.text: Pepsico India Holdings (P) Ltd. v. Food Inspector [(2011) 1 SCC 176]
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
6. In this case, admittedly, the laboratory for the analysis of food item was not defined and no validated method of analysis of the food item was prescribed as mandated under Section 23 (1-A)
(ee) and (hh) of the P.F.A. Act.

Therefore, Ext. P13 report of analysis cannot be acted upon to hold that the food item purchased in this case was adulterated in view of the decision of the Apex court in Pepsico India Holdings (supra).

It was held by the Supreme Court in Pepsico India Holdings (supra)
that since the Laboratories were not notified and the tests conducted by such laboratories were not admissible in evidence, no prosecution could be based on such report and the accused was entitled to get acquittal.

In the decision of this Court in Gopalakrishnan v. Food Inspector [2013 (3) KLT 455], the court relied on the decision of the Supreme Court in Pepsico India Holdings (supra) and found that the Public Analyst's report was not admissible in evidence and accordingly, the Court acquitted the accused.

The matter was referred to a Division Bench and the Division Bench also affirmed the said decision, submitted by the learned counsel for the petitioner and the learned K.Natarajan vs S.Sudarsanan on 7 January, 2016 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/6412785/
2

entities.text: K.Natarajan vs S.Sudarsanan on 7 January, 2016 Indian Kanoon
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: Public Prosecutor.

Even otherwise, in view of the decision of the Pepsico India Holdings (supra), the conviction in this case cannot be sustained as no laboratory was notified and no validated method of analysis was specified as mandated under Section 23 (1-A) (ee) and (hh) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954.

In the result, this Revision Petition stands allowed setting aside the conviction and sentence passed by the courts below under Section Sections 2(ia)(a)(f), 7(i) and 16 (1)(a)(i) of the PFA Act, 1954 and the revision petitioner is acquitted for the said offence.
The bail bond of the revision petitioner stands cancelled and he is set at liberty.
